items.ig_caption:
Two poisoned releases of Microsoft's AI agent framework. 33 minutes apart. 🐍

What SecurityWeek and GitHub's advisory reported (18 Nov):
→ Versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 of the agent-framework package on PyPI carried a credential stealer, published on 17 Nov
→ The package builds AI agents and multi-agent apps and gets about 190,000 downloads a month
→ A .pth startup hook ran at every Python start, even if your code never imported the package
→ It hunted secrets in environment variables and credential files: Azure, AWS, GitHub, Hugging Face, OpenAI, npm and CI tokens
→ Both versions are removed from PyPI; 1.26.0 and earlier are not affected; how the releases were published is still unknown

My take: An official package name is not a trust signal. I'd pin AI agent libraries to hashes and keep cloud and CI tokens out of build steps that run pip install.

What to do: search dev machines, CI runners and container images for 1.26.1 / 1.26.2. If found, treat the environment as exposed: rotate every credential it could reach (including CI and GitHub Actions secrets) and rebuild.

cover.sub: TYPO3 says CVE-2026-125160 is actively exploited. Fixes shipped 17 Nov, alongside 9 more advisories.

slides.title: The flaw
slides.body: CVE-2026-125160 in the TYPO3 Form Framework. When a form upload failed to save, the raw error was shown to the visitor, revealing the storage path, including the 'unguessable' upload folder name.

slides.title: Why it matters
slides.body: Per TYPO3, attackers can then work out the public URL of files they upload through the form. If a form accepts HTML or other browser-run files, that can lead to cross-site scripting where the upload folder has no strict CSP.

slides.label: TYPO3 security advisories in one release (SA-2026-025 to 034)
slides.note: TYPO3's own wording on this one: 'known to be actively exploited'.

TYPO3 CVE-2026-125160: a Form Framework info leak rated Medium, but TYPO3 says it is actively exploited. Failed uploads exposed the hidden upload path. Fixed in 14.3.12, 13.4.40 and ELTS releases.

#PatchNow #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
Rated Medium. Already exploited. 🧩

What TYPO3's advisory says (17 Nov):
→ CVE-2026-125160 is in the Form Framework: when a form upload failed to save, the raw error showed the visitor the storage path
→ That path includes the 'unguessable' upload folder, so attackers can work out the public URL of files they upload
→ If a form accepts HTML or other browser-run files, that can become cross-site scripting where the upload folder lacks a strict CSP
→ TYPO3: "This vulnerability is known to be actively exploited"
→ It shipped in the same release as 9 other TYPO3 security advisories

My take: Medium severity plus active exploitation beats critical-but-theoretical. I'd patch this before the scarier scores, then check your upload folders really get a strict CSP.

What to do: update to TYPO3 14.3.12 LTS or 13.4.40 LTS (ELTS: 12.4.52, 11.5.57, 10.4.63). On nginx, set the upload-folder CSP yourself; the shipped .htaccess only covers Apache.

items.ig_caption:
43 credit unions. One banking platform. 🏦

What The Irish Times (17 Nov) and RTÉ (18 Nov) reported:
→ A suspected data breach hit 43 Irish credit unions; about 40 breach notifications reached the Data Protection Commission, RTÉ reports
→ The provider is understood to be Wellington IT, whose banking platform serves more than a third of Irish credit unions
→ The Irish Times understands hackers exploited a vulnerability in the company's software
→ RTÉ: payees' names, account numbers and addresses may have been compromised; the Irish League of Credit Unions says balances were not, and the flaw is closed
→ The Irish Times says up to 1.8 million people could be affected; the investigation is ongoing

My take: When one platform serves a third of a sector, its flaw is everyone's breach. I'd ask key suppliers how fast they would tell you, and put it in the contract.

What to do: if you're a member, treat any call or email quoting your real payees with suspicion and contact your credit union directly. If you run a supplier programme, map which vendors hold customer data for many firms at once.
